{"id":"jmap-chat-spec-dhv2","title":"JMAP Core has no client language preference: specify how a client asks for a language for localized and server-written text","description":"Split out of jmap-chat-spec-qb21 (2026-11-15). Not Chat-specific: JMAP Core (RFC 8620) has no way for a client to say which language(s) it wants, so every JMAP extension that wants localized server output would have to invent one. Fix it once, generically.

Today:
- RFC 8620 has no request-side language. Server-written text (method-level and SetError 'description', HTTP-level problem details) carries no language tag either.
- Data types that carry several languages (JSCalendar/JSContact 'localizations', and qb21's proposal for Chat, Space, etc.) return all of them and leave the choice to the client. That works, but it costs bandwidth and every client reimplements BCP 47 lookup (RFC 4647).
- Accept-Language (RFC 9110 s12.5.4) exists on the HTTP POST, but RFC 8620 gives it no meaning, it is per-HTTP-request rather than per-session, and it does not reach the EventSource or WebSocket (RFC 8887) push channels.

Options to weigh:
1. Say Accept-Language on the API request is honoured (MAY) for server-written text, and Content-Language on the response tags it. Smallest change; nothing new on the wire. Doesn't cover push.
2. A request-level 'language' (BCP 47 priority list) next to 'using' in the Request object, or a core capability argument. Covers WebSocket; needs a Core extension or erratum-level change.
3. An account/session preference (a JMAP 'UserPreference' or similar settings object), so servers can also localize push notification text when no request is in flight. Overlaps with push-platform guides.
4. A get-time selector: a 'language' argument to /get that collapses 'localizations' into the base properties server-side. Optional; clients that want all languages omit it.

Keyword strength per bcp14-keyword-discipline: everything here is MAY/SHOULD; clients that send nothing get today's behaviour.

Deliverable: decide which option(s), then either a short standalone draft (draft-atwood-jmap-language-00 or similar) or a jmap@ietf.org thread first to see if the WG wants it in Core. Chat (qb21) and mimid-1wgh.51 should cite whatever this settles rather than each defining an Accept-Language rule.

{"description":"Write draft-atwood-jmap-i18n-00: one document that brings language, locale and Unicode handling to the existing JMAP specs we don't control. Re-scoped 2026-11-15 from "JMAP Core has no client language preference" (Mark: "could we just write one ID that applies all this to existing jmap specs?"). Precedent for one document updating many RFCs: RFC 8996.

Header: Updates: 8620 (Core), 8621 (Mail), 9425 (Quotas), 9610 (Contacts), 9670 (Sharing); JMAP Calendars as an Informative reference only if it is still a draft (check status). Check other JMAP RFCs (Blob 9404, WebSocket 8887, MDN 9007, Sieve) for display text before finalizing the list.

Structure:

1. Capability (urn:ietf:params:jmap:i18n or similar) gating the wire changes; servers without it ignore them, clients that send nothing get today's behaviour.
   a. Client language preference. Weigh: a BCP 47 priority list on the Request object next to 'using' (covers WebSocket RFC 8887); an account preference so push notification text can be localized when no request is in flight; giving meaning to Accept-Language (RFC 9110 s12.5.4) on the HTTP POST as the minimal fallback (doesn't reach EventSource/WebSocket push). Lookup per RFC 4647.
   b. Server-written text (method-level and SetError 'description', RFC 9457 problem 'detail' (see jmap-chat-spec-hl0h)) is for display/debugging, never parsed; servers MAY localize it per (a) and SHOULD tag its language.
   c. Optional 'language' argument on /get that collapses 'localizations' into the base properties server-side. Clients that want every language omit it.

2. Generic 'locale' and 'localizations' properties, defined once by reuse of JSCalendar RFC 8984 s4.2.8 (locale) and s4.6.1 (localizations: map from language tag to PatchObject over the localizable properties), so any type with display text can adopt them by listing its localizable properties.

3. Applicability, per spec: which properties are localizable.
   - Mail 8621: Mailbox name, Identity name. Message content needs nothing: MIME already carries charset and Content-Language and 8621 exposes both on EmailBodyPart; say so explicitly so it doesn't look like reopening it. Mailbox names are already Net-Unicode (RFC 5198, implies NFC).
   - Quotas 9425: name, description.
   - Contacts 9610: AddressBook name/description. JSContact (RFC 9553) objects already localize; defer to it.
   - Calendars: Calendar name/description; JSCalendar objects already localize; defer.
   - Sharing 9670: Principal name, description.

4. Guidance with no wire change (Updates text, applies without the capability). Keyword strength per bcp14-keyword-discipline: SHOULD/MAY/prose, MUST only where interop breaks.
   - Encoding: I-JSON (RFC 8620 -> RFC 7493) already makes every string UTF-8; extensions SHOULD cite that, not restate "MUST be valid UTF-8".
   - Normalization: servers SHOULD NOT normalize user text they store and forward (signatures, E2EE, diffs); identifiers and keys compare as exact code-point sequences; say whether senders SHOULD send NFC (RFC 5198 precedent).
   - Collation: display-text sorts honour Comparator.collation (RFC 8620 s5.5); collations are already advertised in the core capability's collationAlgorithms, so nothing new is needed. Text filters match case-insensitively per the collation; stemming/tokenization is language-dependent and implementation-defined, and a body or object language lets the server choose an analyzer.
   - Lengths: limits are in UTF-8 octets; anything a server truncates (previews, snippets, push payloads) SHOULD be cut on a grapheme-cluster boundary (UAX #29), never mid-code-point.
   - Names are display text: servers and clients SHOULD NOT give them meaning; meaning goes in a role or other enumerated property (Mailbox 'role' is the precedent).
   - Display names and identifiers: consider PRECIS RFC 8266 (nicknames) for display names and RFC 8264 IdentifierClass for login-like identifiers as SHOULD.
   - Time: wire timestamps stay UTCDate; wall-clock or recurring times SHOULD carry an IANA time zone ID (as JSCalendar does); date/number formatting is client presentation.
   - Security Considerations: confusables (UTS #39) and bidi overrides (UAX #9) in names; clients SHOULD isolate bidi when interpolating a name into UI text (FSI/PDI or <bdi>).

Before writing: post the outline to jmap@ietf.org to see whether the WG wants parts (the request language preference especially) folded into Core instead.

Consumers: jmap-chat-spec-qb21 (JMAP Chat adopts this draft) and mimid-1wgh.51 cite this rather than each inventing an Accept-Language rule.
